plan.title: Kindle vs Paper: Which Helps You Remember More?
plan.description: A quick look at what research says about reading on a Kindle versus a printed book. Learn where paper wins on comprehension and recall, and where it makes no difference.

beats.narration: You finish a novel on your Kindle. A week later, can you say what happened first, and what came next? Research suggests paper readers often can.

A 2018 meta-analysis pulled together 54 experiments. It found an advantage for paper in comprehension. Scientists call this the screen inferiority effect: people often understand and remember less from digital text.
In one study, a long story was read in a print pocket book or on a Kindle. On most tests, readers did the same. Engagement and recall were equal.
The gap showed up in time. Paper readers did better at placing events in order and rebuilding the plot. A static screen gives fewer physical cues, like the thickness of pages, to anchor the story.

props.title: Why order is harder on screen

beats.narration: So which should you pick? For a quick read, a Kindle is fine. For a story or study you need to remember, choose paper, and slow down on any screen.

props.text: To remember the story in order, pick paper.

accuracy.reason: The core claims match the notes (54 experiments, 2018, chronology gap). However, "thickness of pages" is an embellishment, "Paper wins on chronology" generalizes from one small study, and "Engagement and recall were equal" is correct but sits awkwardly beside the meta-analysis.

coverage.reason: It covers only memory and comprehension. The brief asked for portability, eye strain, battery, feel, price and environment, and none of these appear.

structure.reason: The order is clear: hook, meta-analysis, one study, mechanism, takeaway. The beat 2 claim of a paper advantage sits oddly against beat 3 saying readers did the same, and the topic is narrower than the request.

hook_ending.reason: The opening question about recalling what happened first is a strong hook. The ending is a clear takeaway but rather plain.

tone.reason: Conversational, neutral and suited to a US general audience.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary sensibly and the versus table matches the narration. The stat card is thin, the diagram icons (phone, book, clock) are loosely chosen, and the final kinetic text just repeats the narration.

originality.reason: The chronology finding is a specific and less common angle, but the video ignores the practical comparison the viewer likely wants.

instructions.reason: The request was a fair Kindle vs paper comparison, but the video turns into a one-issue memory piece. It offers no takeaway by reader type beyond a quick-read vs remember split.

language.reason: Clean, fluent English with short sentences, and the length is roughly on target.
